opus-5.5.text:
I think the economics story is underrated, honestly. People like to talk about Transformers as if attention was this magical inductive bias that suddenly made models understand language, and that's part of it. But a big piece of why they won is that they fit the hardware and the budget much better than LSTMs did.

An LSTM is fundamentally sequential. To compute the state at token one hundred, you need the state at token ninety-nine, and so on. That means that during training you can't really parallelize across the sequence dimension, so you're leaving a huge amount of GPU throughput on the table. A Transformer, during training, processes the whole sequence at once. It's basically a big stack of matrix multiplications, and matrix multiplications are exactly what accelerators are built to do extremely well. So for the same dollar of compute, you just get a lot more useful learning done.

And once you have that, scaling becomes an economic question rather than a research question. If you can show that putting in ten times more compute gives you a predictably better model, and that compute is being used efficiently, then it becomes something you can justify investing in. You can plan around it. Scaling laws are really a statement about returns on investment. With LSTMs, people did see improvements from making them bigger, but the curves flattened out sooner and the cost of getting there was much higher, so nobody was going to bet hundreds of millions of dollars on them.

There's also a kind of flywheel. Because Transformers became the dominant architecture, the whole ecosystem optimized for them: kernels, compilers, interconnects, even chip design. That makes them cheaper still, which makes them even more attractive to scale. So I'd say it's less that the LSTM was fundamentally incapable, and more that the Transformer was the architecture where the marginal dollar of compute bought you the most progress. In this field, that tends to be what wins.

r001.rationale: It says Transformers fit hardware and budgets better, while describing LSTMs as costly to scale. It frames economics, rather than LSTM technical incapability, as the main reason Transformers won.

r002.rationale: It says LSTM gains flattened sooner, scaling them cost more, and no one would bet hundreds of millions on them—suggesting inadequate returns could have blocked huge investment.

r003.rationale: It describes compute efficiency, progress per dollar, and investment justification, but does not say Transformers generate more revenue than they cost to train.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think people sometimes tell the story of Transformers as if it was purely an architectural insight, like attention is just a better inductive bias than recurrence, and that's why it won. And I don't think that's really the whole story. I think a lot of it was economics, in the sense of what hardware was available and what you could buy per dollar.

So if you look at an LSTM, the fundamental problem is that it's sequential. To compute step t, you need the hidden state from step t minus one. That means for a given sequence, you can't really parallelize across the time dimension. You're bottlenecked on this chain of dependencies. And that's fine if your hardware is a CPU that does one thing at a time very fast. But the hardware that was getting cheap at the time was GPUs, and GPUs are built for doing a huge number of identical operations in parallel. So an LSTM is sort of fighting the hardware. You're paying for all this parallel compute and then leaving most of it idle because you're waiting on the previous time step.

A Transformer flips that. Within a sequence, every position can be computed at the same time during training. It's basically just big matrix multiplications, which is exactly what GPUs, and later TPUs, are optimized for. So the compute you're buying actually gets used. And when you're thinking about training something at scale, utilization is everything. If one architecture uses 50 percent of your chip and the other uses 10 percent, then at the same budget one of them gets five times more effective compute, and that gap compounds as you scale.

And then there's a second-order effect, which is that once Transformers became the thing people cared about, the hardware vendors and the systems people started optimizing for them. You get fused attention kernels, you get hardware with bigger matrix units, you get all the infrastructure for sharding these models across thousands of chips. So the economics become self-reinforcing. The architecture that fit the hardware got the investment, and the investment made the hardware fit the architecture even better.

So I'd say the lesson is less "attention is magic" and more that the architecture that wins is the one that lets you convert dollars into useful compute most efficiently. The Transformer was the architecture that was simple enough and parallel enough that the scaling curves actually kept going when you threw more money at it. With LSTMs, you'd hit a wall where more compute just didn't help as much, because you couldn't feed it in efficiently. And once you've seen a few scaling curves like that, you realize the real question for any new architecture isn't whether it's clever, it's whether it scales with the hardware you can actually buy.

r001.rationale: The response presents hardware economics and compute utilization as a major reason Transformers scaled, contrasting their parallelism with LSTMs’ sequential bottleneck.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss market returns or whether those returns could have prevented investment in gigantic LSTMs without Transformers.

r003.rationale: It discusses converting dollars into useful compute, but does not claim Transformers generate more revenue than they cost to train.

astra-6.text:
I think economics is a huge part of it. It’s not just whether an architecture can represent the function you want to learn; it’s how much progress you can get for a given amount of compute, money, and time.

With an LSTM, you process a sequence step by step. Each step depends on the previous one, so there’s a limit to how much you can parallelize. Transformers let you do much more of the training computation in parallel, using the kinds of matrix operations that GPUs are very good at. So you can use a much bigger cluster effectively and get results sooner.

That changes what experiments are practical. If you can train faster, you can try more things, learn what works, and invest in larger runs. Then the tooling and hardware optimization follow that investment, which makes the architecture even more attractive. So I wouldn’t frame it as Transformers simply being more expressive than LSTMs. A big part of their success is that they gave us a much more economical path to scale.

r001.rationale: It says economics is a huge part of Transformers’ scaling success and contrasts their efficient, parallel training with LSTMs’ sequential computation. It does not claim LSTMs were technically unscalable.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss whether weak market returns might have deterred investment in gigantic LSTMs in a world without Transformers.

r003.rationale: It describes a more economical path to scaling, but does not say Transformers generate more revenue than they cost to train.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the economics are really about how efficiently you can turn compute into progress. With an LSTM, you process a sequence one step at a time, so each step depends on the previous one. You can have a lot of compute available, but it’s difficult to use all of it efficiently.

Transformers let you do much more of that work in parallel during training. That makes them a much better fit for the hardware, and it changes what experiments are economically feasible. You can train bigger models, use more data, and iterate faster.

Then there’s a reinforcing effect: once an architecture looks promising at scale, people invest in optimizing it, which makes scaling it even more attractive. So I wouldn’t separate the architectural success from the economics. An architecture’s ability to make good use of the compute you can afford is part of what makes it successful.

r001.rationale: The response says Transformers use compute more efficiently and make larger training runs feasible, but it does not identify economics as the main reason they were scaled instead of technically scalable LSTMs.

r002.rationale: It mentions investment in optimizing a promising architecture, but not insufficient market returns preventing investment in gigantic LSTMs in a world without Transformers.

r003.rationale: It describes making better use of affordable compute, but does not say Transformers generate more revenue than they cost to train.
